title: Why Does Earth Have a Magnetic Field?
narration: Mid-flight over the Atlantic, Ada watches her cockpit compass needle swing three degrees off north.
That needle isn't broken. Bolt taps the glass — and it actually wants to tilt downward too.
So one question follows Ada the whole flight. Why does Earth have a magnetic field — and why won't it fade?
Maybe Earth is a giant iron bar magnet? No. Iron loses all magnetism above 770 degrees — and the core is far hotter.
We'll trace it in three layers. The surface Ada feels, the engine that makes it, and deep time that nearly ended it.
Quick guess for later. If this shield weakens, what's the real danger — a broken compass, fried satellites, or the air itself?
Ada lands. Bolt lifts her compass to a wall map — the needle points at a magnetic pole hundreds of kilometres off the real one.
Therefore every chart she's ever flown carries a printed correction. The magnetic pole and the true pole simply disagree.
But that pole won't hold still. It has crept over a thousand kilometres across the Arctic in a single lifetime.
A wandering pole means the source isn't fixed rock. It's something fluid, moving. Bolt leads Ada's gaze straight down through the floor.
Beneath the crust sits a core of molten iron larger than Mars. Its churning is what her needle has been chasing.
But hot liquid iron alone still isn't magnetic. So what turns molten metal into a planet-sized magnet?
The answer needs three things at once. Bolt marks them on the compass rim — a conducting fluid, heat, and spin.
For a moment it feels solved. Three ingredients, done. But each does a specific job — pull one, and everything shuts off.
Ingredient one. The inner core is slowly freezing solid, releasing heat outward — and that forces the liquid outer core to churn upward.
Therefore huge columns of molten iron rise, cool, and sink in endless loops. The core is in permanent, restless motion.
But straight up-and-down loops wouldn't twist into anything. You need something to bend those columns sideways.
Earth's daily spin does it. Rotation drags the rising iron into corkscrewing spirals, all leaning the same way.
Bolt spins Ada's compass on the table. The needle traces a spiral, not a line.
Here's the thing. Moving molten iron carries electric current — and flowing current always wraps a magnetic field around itself.
This self-sustaining loop has a name. The geodynamo — where a field makes currents that make more field.
But that's a trap. You need a field to make the field — so where did the first one come from?
A tiny seed field from the young solar system was enough. The spinning core amplified that faint whisper into a roar.
Bolt gives Ada a metaphor she'll keep. The core is a bicycle dynamo — rotation is the wheel that never stops.
So the field isn't a battery draining down. It's rebuilt every single second the core keeps churning.
Now the reach explodes. The field balloons tens of thousands of kilometres out into open space.
And out there it meets the Sun's storm. Charged particles slam toward the planet at over a million kilometres per hour.
The field deflects the flood around Earth. And the danger you guessed at? It was never the compass.
Without this shield, the solar wind slowly strips our air away over time. The field is why we still have a thick atmosphere.
Ada sees the proof at night. Particles leaking through the poles crash into the sky and set it glowing.
But if it depends on a hot, molten core, it can't last forever. This engine has a lifespan.
Bolt lays Mars beside Earth. Mars once had a field too — and a thicker sky, with liquid water.
Being small, Mars cooled fast. Its churning core lost its dynamo, and the field simply stopped.
That dead red world is a warning. A stopped engine, a stolen sky. Earth's possible ending.
But wait. Has Earth's field always been steady, always pointing the same way it does now? Guess.
Most people assume yes. But the ocean floor keeps a stranger record, frozen inside its iron grains.
When lava cools at ocean ridges, its iron locks onto whichever way the field points. A snapshot.
Bolt runs Ada's finger across the striped seafloor. North. South. North. South. All recorded in stone.
Those alternating stripes mean the poles have completely flipped. North becoming south. Hundreds of times.
And they never keep a schedule. Sometimes millions of years apart. Sometimes only tens of thousands.
Here's the strange part. A flip isn't a clean switch. The field weakens, splinters into several weak poles, then rebuilds backwards. The shield partly drops for centuries.
But the rocks offer relief. Even through those chaotic centuries, the field never fully vanished. Life carried on.
Ada exhales. The atmosphere survived every reversal. A scrambled field still beats no field at all.
But her compass carries a warning. Its strength has dropped several percent in just two centuries.
And a strange dent has grown over the South Atlantic. Satellites already flicker and glitch flying through it.
So put it together. A wandering pole, a weakening field, a growing weak spot. Early tremors of a flip beginning now?
But a flip unfolds over thousands of years. Not one flight. Ada will never see it finish. Neither will her grandchildren.
The real hostage during a weak spell isn't her compass. It's every satellite, power grid, and pipeline exposed to raw solar particles.
Nearly three thousand kilometres down, the engine never rests. The inner core keeps freezing.
So the field will rebuild, as it always has. A flip is stumbling, not dying.
Earth has a magnetic field for one reason. Molten iron, churning, spinning, freezing at once.
That drift in Ada's needle? That breathable sky above her? Both pour from the same core.
Bolt sets the compass down. The needle settles, glowing with a pulse from far below.
Ada looks at the needle differently now. A receipt from a fire older than the planet's crust.
The field is really a heartbeat. And someday, long after us, that heart goes still.
